clinicalPearls: Degenerative tendinopathy of the gluteus medius and minimus tendons at the greater trochanter, the principal cause of greater trochanteric pain syndrome
Presents with lateral hip pain aggravated by lying on the side, single-leg loading, stairs and prolonged standing
Predominantly affects women in middle to older age
Provocative tests include resisted hip abduction, prolonged single-leg stance and adduction or FABER tests
Compressive load from hip adduction combined with tensile overload drives the tendon change; it is degenerative rather than inflammatory
Ultrasound and MRI confirm tendinopathy and detect tears and secondary bursal change
Management is education, load modification to avoid adduction and compression, and progressive abductor loading with physiotherapy
Corticosteroid injection gives only short-term benefit, and shockwave therapy may help resistant cases
reference.pathophysiology: The gluteus medius and minimus tendons insert on the greater trochanter and act as key hip abductors and pelvic stabilisers. Combined compressive load, generated when the hip adducts and the iliotibial band presses the tendon against the trochanter, and tensile overload lead to a degenerative tendinopathy with disorganised collagen and failed healing, often with secondary thickening of the adjacent bursae. This underlies most presentations of greater trochanteric pain syndrome, and advanced disease may progress to partial- or full-thickness abductor tendon tears.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbar radiculopathy or referred spinal pain
Femoral neck or greater trochanter stress fracture
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound to assess tendon integrity and tears and bursal change and to guide injection
MRI to characterise tendinopathy and tears and exclude hip or bony pathology
Plain radiographs of the pelvis and hip for joint and bony assessment
Clinical tests (resisted abduction, single-leg stance, adduction or FABER)
Lumbar spine assessment for referred pain
redFlags: Marked abductor weakness or a Trendelenburg gait suggesting a significant tendon tear
Rest or night bone pain or systemic features suggesting infection or malignancy
History suggesting a femoral neck stress fracture
reference.prognosis: Structured education and abductor loading achieve good outcomes in most; symptoms can be persistent, and confirmed full-thickness tears may warrant surgical repair.
pitfalls: Treating as simple 'bursitis' and relying on rest or injection rather than loading
Overlooking referred pain from the lumbar spine
Provocative side-lying positions and adduction stretches that compress and aggravate the tendon
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Centre treatment on patient education and a progressive gluteal abductor loading and strengthening programme delivered by physiotherapy, the mainstay of care
Reduce compressive load by advising against hip adduction postures such as sitting cross-legged, standing hanging on one hip and side-lying on the affected side
Modify aggravating activity and use short-term simple analgesia to allow rehabilitation to proceed
Consider an ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection for short-term pain relief when symptoms limit engagement with exercise, recognising the benefit is temporary
Consider adjuncts such as platelet-rich plasma or extracorporeal shockwave therapy in refractory cases
Refer for surgical assessment and abductor tendon repair when a confirmed full-thickness tear fails conservative management
Assess and manage the lumbar spine and hip joint for contributing referred pain or coexisting pathology
